en: Title: *Sattvārādhanastava* Author: Nāgārjuna Source:

Compiled from Lévi 1929, pp. 264–265 (based on NAK 3-715 = NGMPP B 23/8) and a manuscript fragment identified by Szántó (NAK 5-135 = NGMPP B 24/56); based on a new edition by Cheung, forthcoming; pagination according to this edition.
Devotion to the welfare of sentient beings alone is my devotion; all else is non-devotion.
He does not abandon his compassion for sentient beings, nor for me;
yet, as he wanders having set aside that compassion, it is compassion alone—and nothing else—that ought to uplift those lapses of his. (1)
Therefore I have been honored by him— he who bears the burden of my teaching, whose activity toward sentient beings is permeated with compassion,
and who possesses ethical discipline, learning, compassion, and keen intelligence.
He who possesses [this] has indeed always honored the Sugata.
For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, I have attained perfection;
for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings alone, I bear this body.
How can he who harms living beings even in his mind rely upon me alone— he who is indifferent toward me?
That indeed is worship which, even when directed toward the welfare of sentient beings, brings satisfaction to the mind of the one being worshipped;
whereas that which is violent in nature, or arises from the intent to harm others, is not.
Even when consecrated by ritual, worship does not follow that which is worshipped.
Wives, sons, wealth, great power, and sovereignty;
flesh, blood, the eyes, and the body—all these are subject to the power of the self.
Those for whose sake I have renounced [everything]—
if anyone harms them, by that I am harmed;
for my supreme worship consists in benefiting sentient beings.

And there would be defeat consisting in the supreme injury to sentient beings. For one who strikes at those beings toward whom he desires happiness—which is equal for all beings as suffering is equal for all—[he brings about their ruin]. (6)
Having encountered sentient beings, I have performed virtuous deeds and propitiated the Protectors;
I have attained the perfections while remaining dedicated solely to the welfare of the assembly of sentient beings.
With a mind striving for the welfare of sentient beings, the power of Māra was shattered;
by sentient beings themselves, in such and such ways, they were so fashioned that I was made a Buddha.
In what object here should compassion and loving-kindness be perfected, and upon what should they be focused?
Where would there be objects such as equanimity and sympathetic joy? In what [realm] would the liberations and so forth exist?
For what purpose would one who possesses a compassionate mind have cultivated patience for so long, if living beings were not friends in the act of affection throughout birth after birth? (8)

It was sentient beings alone who, having entered the states of elephants and other forms, were given away by me many times; and it was sentient beings alone who, having become worthy recipients, were made to accept what was to be given.
By sentient beings alone, through their passage into various states of existence, my compassion has been increased.
If I do not protect sentient beings themselves, for whose sake has any benefit been accomplished?
If living beings were not made one's own by having reached the world of Yama through the mockery of the whirlpools of birth in this saṃsāra, which is so full of the onset of calamities.
This crossing over from saṃsāra and this most wonderful majesty of the Sugata—
by what purpose would it be desired, were sentient beings not dear to me?
And as long as this teaching of mine, the teaching for the world, continues to blaze forth...
Therefore, you who are self-possessed and devoted to the welfare of others should remain steadfast;
having repeatedly heard of my conduct for the sake of sentient beings, you must not grow weary, nor should you treat this body— which has now been spoken of as its essence exhausted— with neglect.
O Anu, by those who carry [you].
